newsitem.title: USA: Freeh mounts big hunt for stolen FBI weapons.
newsitem.headline: Freeh mounts big hunt for stolen FBI weapons.

text.p: The FBI has mounted a major effort to recover a vanload of M-16 rifles, ammunition and other assault gear stolen from one of its SWAT teams in Memphis, Tennessee, but has so far come up empty-handed, FBI Director Louis Freeh told Congress on Wednesday.

"We certainly have put on a full-court press to immediately retrieve and find those weapons -- very dangerous weapons," Freeh told a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing. He said a task force of FBI agents and state and local authorities were hunting for the arsenal taken from a van that belonged to a visiting FBI team from Little Rock, Arkansas.

The van was stolen from the parking lot of a hotel where the Little Rock team had spent Monday night. Its burned-out shell was found early on Tuesday in Millington, about about 15 miles (24 km) north of Memphis.
"We can't account for the weapons," Freeh said in reply to a question from Sen. Fred Thompson, a Tennessee Republican.

Freeh said the van had been left unattended in the parking lot with no special locks on the weapons and no burglar alarm. He said an internal investigation was under way to determine whether the FBI personnel involved had ignored any safety rules by leaving it in an unguarded area overnight.
Among the missing weapons were tear gas launchers, a shotgun and other equipment for a training exercise in Memphis being attended by about half a dozen federal special weapons and tactics squads.

Freeh said FBI agents typically parked such vans in guarded areas such as police stations when they were on the road overnight. He said investigators would look into whether more specific safeguards were required.

Judiciary Committee members at the hearing generally voiced confidence in Freeh's stewardship despite the bureau's role in improperly providing hundreds of confidential personnel files to the Clinton White House, problems at its once-vaunted crime laboratory and other recent criticisms.
"You have my confidence, and we must ensure that all share my view," Committee Chairman Orrin Hatch, a Utah Republican, said in his opening statement.

But Sen. Charles Grassley, an Iowa Republican, accused Freeh of trying to mislead Congress and the public about warning signs of problems at the crime lab and of seeking "to shoot" the whistleblower rather than fix the problem.
"I see it as an effort to get at a bearer of bad news. I think what Dr. Whitehurst was talking about for eight years you saw as hurting the FBI's image," Grassley said.

Frederic Whitehurst, a chemist in the explosives laboratory, was largely responsible for forcing a Justice Department inspector general's investigation of the lab by filing repeated complaints since 1989 about its failings.

Freeh, who took over the bureau in September 1993 as the seriousness of the laboratory's problems began to emerge, said he took "great exception" to Grassley's charge that Freeh had knowingly misled anyone about the matter.
